reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Portal hypertension is a sustained rise in portal venous pressure and is most often caused by cirrhosis in the developed world and by schistosomiasis or portal vein thrombosis elsewhere
Clinical consequences arise from portosystemic collaterals and splanchnic congestion: gastro-oesophageal varices, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, ascites, and caput medusae
Variceal haemorrhage is the most dangerous complication and presents as haematemesis or melaena, often with haemodynamic instability

Causes are usefully grouped as prehepatic (e.g. portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (presinusoidal, sinusoidal as in cirrhosis, or postsinusoidal), and posthepatic (e.g. Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis)
Endoscopy characterises and treats varices, while non-selective beta-blockade reduces portal pressure and the risk of first or recurrent bleeding
Acute variceal bleeding is managed with resuscitation, vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic band ligation, and antibiotic prophylaxis, with balloon tamponade or TIPS as rescue
Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) and, less commonly, surgical shunts decompress the portal system but can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Portal hypertension results from increased resistance to portal blood flow combined with increased splanchnic inflow. In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort the hepatic architecture and raise sinusoidal resistance, compounded by intrahepatic vasoconstriction. Splanchnic arterial vasodilatation, mediated in part by nitric oxide, increases portal inflow and sustains the elevated pressure. As pressure rises, portosystemic collateral channels open at sites of communication between the portal and systemic circulations, producing varices at the gastro-oesophageal junction, rectum, and anterior abdominal wall. Splenic congestion causes splenomegaly and hypersplenism, and the combination of portal hypertension and hepatic dysfunction drives ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis (posthepatic)
Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension / idiopathic portal hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Upper GI endoscopy to grade and treat varices
Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler of the portal and hepatic veins to assess flow, thrombosis, and splenomegaly
Liver function tests, coagulation profile, and full blood count (for hypersplenism-related cytopenias)
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for hepatic architecture, collaterals, and vascular patency
Hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement where available to quantify portal pressure
Liver biopsy or elastography to assess fibrosis and clarify aetiology
redFlags: Active variceal haemorrhage with haematemesis, melaena, and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency resuscitation and endoscopy
Encephalopathy with reduced consciousness and risk of aspiration
Rapidly accumulating tense ascites or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Signs of decompensation (jaundice, coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome) indicating advanced liver failure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is dominated by the underlying liver disease and by whether decompensation has occurred; variceal bleeding carries substantial mortality, particularly in advanced cirrhosis. Effective prophylaxis, endoscopic therapy, and shunting reduce rebleeding, but long-term survival depends on hepatic reserve and, in suitable candidates, transplantation.
pitfalls: Over-transfusing during variceal bleeding, which can raise portal pressure and worsen haemorrhage
Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients with gastrointestinal bleeding
Aggressive correction of coagulopathy or platelet counts without regard to the rebalanced haemostasis of cirrhosis
Creating a shunt without anticipating precipitation or worsening of hepatic encephalopathy
Attributing all upper GI bleeding to varices and missing coexisting peptic ulceration or portal hypertensive gastropathy
